analysis.one_liner: Bans mandatory arbitration clauses in cellphone, cable, and internet service contracts.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote; it died in the Senate Judiciary Committee when the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: Wireless carriers, cable and satellite TV companies, and internet providers write fine-print clauses into their service contracts requiring customers to settle any dispute with a private arbitrator, one person at a time, and giving up the right to go to court or join a class action. This bill would make those clauses unenforceable for telecommunications services, so consumers could sue in court and band together in class actions. It also says a court, not the arbitrator, decides whether the clause applies, and it leaves union collective bargaining agreements alone.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers with cellphone, cable, satellite TV, internet, or phone service contracts. When a company bills thousands of customers small wrongful fees, individual arbitration clauses make it uneconomical for any one customer to fight; a class action is the only realistic remedy. The bill would restore access to court and class actions for those disputes, and would put the decision on whether the arbitration clause applies in a judge's hands instead of the arbitrator's.

how_it_helps.text: No predispute arbitration clause would be valid or enforceable for disputes over commercial mobile service, multichannel video programming (cable/satellite), telecommunications or information services, or other common-carrier services under the Communications Act.

Whether the bill applies to a given arbitration clause, and whether that clause is valid, would be decided by a court under federal law rather than by an arbitrator, closing a loophole where the arbitrator decides his own authority.

The bill does not touch arbitration in union collective bargaining agreements, except that no such provision can waive an employee's right to go to court to enforce rights under the Constitution, statutes, or public policy.

analysis.who_pays: Telecommunications and cable companies, which would lose the arbitration clauses they use to keep consumer disputes out of court and to avoid class-wide liability for billing errors, overcharges, and service failures. They would face more consumer lawsuits and potentially larger payouts.

drawbacks.text: Supporters of forced arbitration argue it resolves consumer disputes faster and cheaper than court, and that removing it could raise the cost of providing service and be passed on to customers. Class actions can also return little to individual class members while paying large fees to plaintiffs' attorneys.

The bill covers only telecommunications services, so the same arbitration clauses would remain enforceable in credit cards, bank accounts, employment contracts, and many other consumer agreements, leaving most of the problem untouched.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For consumers, the benefit is real: arbitration clauses in telecom contracts effectively eliminate recovery in small-dollar, widespread-harm cases, and class action is the only tool that fits them. The honest costs are that litigation is slower and more expensive than arbitration for an individual dispute, and that some of the industry's compliance costs could flow into prices. The narrow scope—telecom only, while the same clauses persist across the rest of consumer life—makes it a partial fix rather than a structural one.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never held a hearing or vote on it; it died there when the 114th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Blumenthal introduced the bill on April 28, 2016, joined by seven original cosponsors (six Democrats and Independent Sen. Sanders).
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary on the day of introduction.
No further action appears in the bill's history: no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action. The 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017, and the bill expired.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Telecom and cable companies are better off, because they kept the mandatory arbitration clauses that prevent customers from joining class actions over billing errors and overcharges. Consumers with grievances against those companies are left with the same fine print as before.

for.name: Sen. Richard Blumenthal
for.role: Senate sponsor (D-CT), member of the Judiciary Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to bar forced arbitration clauses in telecommunications service contracts.

for.name: Eight Senate cosponsors
for.role: Original cosponsors (7 D or I): Franken, Brown, Whitehouse, Markey, Sanders, Merkley, Warren
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction; all were Democrats or Independents.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Never took up the bill; the record shows no hearing, markup, or vote after the April 2016 referral.

against.name: Sen. Chuck Grassley
against.what_they_did: As chair, did not schedule any hearing or markup of the bill, leaving it unacted on for the remainder of the Congress.

against.name: Telecom, cable, and business groups
against.role: Industry that uses mandatory arbitration clauses
against.what_they_did: Opposed legislative limits on forced arbitration in consumer contracts, which would expose them to class-action liability.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor was a Democrat or Independent; no Republican signed on, and the Republican-run Judiciary Committee gave the bill no action.

industries.industry: Wireless, cable, satellite, and internet service providers
industries.note: These companies put arbitration clauses in nearly every service contract, blocking customers from banding together in class actions over small-dollar overcharges and billing errors. The bill would have stripped that protection, exposing them to consumer suits in court. Their interest in keeping disputes individual and private runs directly against customers' ability to recover.

Arbitration firms earn fees from the mandatory clauses written into consumer telecom contracts. The bill would shrink that business, though it would also remove the clause-interpretation work that flows to arbitrators today.
